sources.claim: Registering a business name with a state, a DBA, or a domain name is not the same as trademark rights; trademark protection is a separate process.

sections.skill: Explain what a DBA does and does not do

questions.prompt: Maria Lopez sells cakes as "Sunny Bakes." What does a DBA filing let her do?

choices.text: Turn her business into an LLC without other filings
Stop all others from using "Sunny Bakes" nationwide
Protect her house from business debts

questions.intro: A DBA ("doing business as"), also called a trade name, assumed name or fictitious name, lets a business operate under a name different from its legal name. A sole proprietor named Maria Lopez who sells as "Sunny Bakes" may need to register that name; so may an LLC operating under a different name. Where it is filed (state, county or city) depends on the location. A DBA does NOT create a new entity, does NOT give liability protection, and does NOT give trademark rights. Check local rules.
questions.feedback: A DBA registers a name the business uses.

sections.skill: A name tag, not a new person

questions.prompt: A DBA is most like what?
questions.intro: A DBA is like a name tag. If Robert wears a tag saying "Coach Bob," he is still Robert. The tag tells people what to call him at work; it does not make him a different person or give him special protection. A business with a DBA is still the same business, with the same owner, the same responsibilities and the same legal form. It simply uses another name with customers.
questions.feedback: It is just a name used publicly.
